question: Two cores each hold a copy of variable x in their own caches. After core 0 writes x, what problem could occur when core 1 reads x if there were no cache coherence mechanism?
choices: Core 1 reads the stale value left in its own cache
Core 1's read is always faster than core 0's write
x is read as double its value
explanation: In a multicore CPU, each core's cache can hold a copy of the same address. If core 0 updates x only in its own cache, core 1's cache keeps the old value and core 1 reads it. A cache coherence mechanism, for example by invalidating other cores' copies on a write, ensures that every core sees the latest value.
choiceNotes: Correct. The copies fall out of sync.
It is a question of correctness, not speed.
Values do not change by themselves.

question: Which correctly lists the four states of the MESI cache coherence protocol?
choices: Memory, Execute, Store, Index
Modified, Exclusive, Shared, Invalid
Miss, Evict, Swap, Idle
explanation: In MESI, each cache line is in one of four states: Modified (changed and held only by this core), Exclusive (unchanged and held only by this core), Shared (several cores hold the same contents) or Invalid. The state changes whenever the core reads or writes, or learns of other cores' reads and writes, which prevents copies of the same address from disagreeing.
choiceNotes: These are not cache line states.
Correct. Every line is in one of these four states.
These are not cache line states.

question: In the MESI protocol, what does it mean when a cache line is in the Modified (M) state?
choices: Only this core holds the line, and its contents differ from main memory (it must be written back)
Several cores hold the same contents, which also match main memory
The line's contents are unusable and must be fetched again to read
explanation: The M state means this core has written the line and alone holds the latest value. Main memory is stale, so when the line is evicted or another core wants to read it, the latest value must be written back or supplied directly. A line in M can be written again any number of times without notifying other cores, so repeated writes by the same core are fast.
choiceNotes: Correct. It is written back to memory when evicted.
That is the Shared (S) state.
That is the Invalid (I) state.

question: In the MESI protocol, what happens when a core writes to a line it holds in the Exclusive (E) state?
choices: It sends invalidation requests to all other cores before writing
It cannot write, so it writes to main memory and reads the line back
No other core needs to be notified, and the line simply becomes M
explanation: The E state means only this core holds the line and its contents match main memory. Since there are known to be no other copies, the core can move to M on a write without sending invalidations. The benefit of having E is saving that communication in the common pattern of reading and then writing data used by a single core. Writing from S, by contrast, requires invalidating other copies.
choiceNotes: In E there are no other copies, so no notice is needed.
It can write directly.
Correct. The core knows it is the only holder.

question: In an invalidation-based coherence protocol, what happens when a core writes to a line in the Shared (S) state?
choices: It leaves other copies alone and updates only its own line
It invalidates other cores' copies of the line, then sets its own line to M and writes
It empties every core's cache before writing
explanation: In S, other cores may hold the same line, so writing directly would leave their copies stale. The core sends an invalidation request, putting other copies into I, then sets its own line to M and writes. When another core next reads the data it misses and fetches the latest value. Most CPUs use this invalidation-based approach.
choiceNotes: Other cores would then read stale values.
Correct. It ensures no stale copies remain.
There is no need to clear unrelated lines.

question: In MESI, when core 1 tries to read a line that core 0 holds in the Modified (M) state, what generally happens?
choices: Core 0 writes back or forwards the latest value to core 1, and both lines become Shared (S)
Core 1 reads the stale value from memory, and core 0 stays in M
Core 1's read waits until core 0 eventually evicts the line
explanation: Core 0 sees core 1's read request and, knowing it holds the latest value, writes it back to memory or forwards it directly to core 1. Afterward both cores hold the same contents, so both lines become S. The key is never letting core 1 read the stale value from memory. Forwarding directly delivers the value faster than going through main memory.
choiceNotes: Correct. The latest value becomes shared.
That would break coherence.
It is handled immediately, not on eviction.

question: Which describes the snooping approach to cache coherence?
choices: The OS periodically inspects every cache and fixes discrepancies
Each core's cache watches other cores' reads and writes on a shared bus or similar and updates its own line states
The programmer manually sends values to other cores on each write
explanation: In snooping, every core's read and write requests reach all caches, and each cache checks whether it holds the same line and invalidates it or supplies data. It is simple and suits a small number of cores. As cores increase, broadcasting every request to every cache generates too much traffic, so large systems use directory-based coherence.
choiceNotes: Hardware does it automatically.
Correct. The caches snoop on the traffic.
The programmer need not be involved.

question: Why do systems with many cores use directory-based coherence instead of snooping?
choices: Recording which cores hold each line lets notices go only to the cores involved, reducing traffic
Directory-based coherence makes caches unnecessary
Directory-based coherence can notify all cores on every write
explanation: Directory-based coherence keeps a table (the directory) recording, for each line, which cores hold copies and in what state. On a write, it consults the directory and sends invalidations only to the cores holding copies. With less traffic than snooping, which notifies all caches at once, it is used in CPUs with dozens of cores or more, such as server processors.
choiceNotes: Correct. There is no need to broadcast to everyone.
Caches are still used.
Avoiding broadcast is the whole point.

question: Coherence protocols can be invalidation-based or update-based. Why do most CPUs use invalidation?
choices: When the same core writes a line repeatedly, only the first write needs an invalidation, so traffic is lower
With update-based protocols other cores read stale values
Invalidation doubles cache capacity
explanation: An update-based protocol sends the new value to other copies on every write, which helps if other cores read it soon, but generates traffic on each of a core's repeated writes. With invalidation, after the first write invalidates other copies, further writes to the M line need no communication. Real programs often write repeatedly, so invalidation is the norm.
choiceNotes: Correct. Update-based protocols send the value on every write.
Update-based protocols also stay correct; the issue is traffic.
Capacity does not change.

question: Which describes false sharing in a multithreaded program?
choices: Threads update different variables that sit in the same cache line, so the line bounces between cores and slows things down
Two threads update the same variable without synchronization and corrupt it
Threads wait on each other's locks and stop
explanation: Coherence is managed per cache line, typically 64 bytes. Even if core 0 writes only a and core 1 writes only b, when a and b share a line each write invalidates the other's copy and the line bounces between the cores. The results are correct but performance drops sharply: this is false sharing. It often occurs with arrays of per-thread counters.
choiceNotes: Correct. The data is not shared, but the line is.
That is a data race.
That is a deadlock.

question: False sharing occurs with an array of per-thread counters such as "long cnt[8];". What is the most suitable fix?
choices: Change the counters from long to int to shrink the array
Add padding or alignment so that each counter sits in its own cache line
Increase the number of threads to spread out the waiting
explanation: With 8-byte longs, eight counters fit in a single 64-byte line, and all threads fight over it. Padding so each counter sits 64 bytes apart, or aligning a struct to the cache-line size, gives each thread its own line. Another effective approach is for each thread to count in a local variable and add to the shared location only once at the end.
choiceNotes: Shrinking packs them even more tightly into one line.
Correct. Separating the lines stops the bouncing.
More threads would increase the bouncing.

question: Which describes a data race?
choices: Multiple threads only read the same variable at the same time
One thread writes the same variable twice in a row
Multiple threads access the same variable at the same time without synchronization, and at least one access is a write
explanation: A data race occurs when the order of reads and writes to one location is not fixed by synchronization, so the result depends on the order in which they happened to run. Because it appears or not depending on timing, it is a hard bug to find by testing. In C and C++, a program with a data race has undefined behavior. Locks or atomic variables must be used to establish an order.
choiceNotes: Reading alone changes nothing, so there is no problem.
Within one thread the order is well defined.
Correct. It makes results vary from run to run.

question: When two threads run the code above simultaneously, the final counter can be less than 200000. Why?
choices: Because the CPU sometimes computes the addition incorrectly
counter++ is a separate read, add and write, and when the threads overlap one thread's increment is lost
Because each thread's loop count is automatically halved
explanation: counter++ consists of three operations: read the value from memory, add 1 and write it back. If thread A reads 100 and thread B also reads 100 before A writes back, both write 101, and two increments become one. This is a textbook data race. Using an atomic add instruction, or a lock so only one thread updates at a time, gives the correct 200000.
choiceNotes: The CPU computes correctly.
Correct. Both add 1 to the same old value and write the same result.
The loop count does not change.

question: Which describes an atomic instruction?
choices: An instruction that performs a memory read and write as a single operation that no other core can interrupt partway
An instruction for physics calculations that counts atoms
The fastest instruction, always finishing in one clock
explanation: An atomic instruction performs a read, compute and write sequence such that no other core's access can come in between. Other cores see only the state before or after the operation. Examples include CAS (compare-and-swap), fetch-and-add and RISC-V's LR/SC and AMO instructions, which are the building blocks of locks and lock-free data structures.
choiceNotes: Correct. To other cores it appears to happen instantaneously.
Atomic here means indivisible.
Its defining feature is indivisibility, not speed.

question: What does the atomic CAS (compare-and-swap) instruction do?
choices: It writes a new value only if memory equals an expected value, and reports whether it succeeded
It compares two memory values and writes the larger into both
It swaps a memory value and a register value unconditionally
explanation: CAS atomically performs "if the value at this address is still the expected value, change it to the new value". If another thread changed the value between the read and the write, it fails, so updates proceed only when nothing has interfered. Wrapping it in a loop that rereads, recomputes and retries on failure lets shared values be updated safely without a lock. x86's cmpxchg instruction is an example.
choiceNotes: Correct. Compare, and swap if equal.
It does not write the larger value.
An unconditional swap is the exchange instruction.

question: The code above doubles the shared variable counter using CAS(&p, expected, new). When does the CAS fail so the loop repeats?
choices: When counter is 0
When another thread changes counter between reading old and executing the CAS
When new is larger than old
explanation: CAS writes the new value only if counter still equals the old value read earlier. If another thread changed it meanwhile, the local new was computed from a stale value, so CAS does not write it and reports failure. The loop rereads the latest value and recomputes. A plain addition could use fetch-and-add, but this pattern makes any update, such as doubling, atomic.
choiceNotes: Even with 0 it succeeds if no one else changed it.
Correct. It discards the computation based on the old value and retries.
Relative size is not the failure condition.

question: With an instruction pair such as RISC-V LR/SC (load-reserved / store-conditional), when does the SC fail?
choices: When the value SC writes equals the value LR read
When the reservation is lost, for example because another core wrote that address between the LR and the SC
Whenever any other instruction is executed between LR and SC
explanation: LR reads a value and at the same time "reserves" the address. When SC later writes, it succeeds if the reservation is intact and fails without writing if the reservation was lost, for example because another core wrote there. Whereas CAS checks for a matching value, LR/SC checks whether any write happened, so it also detects a value that changed and changed back. Arm has a similar instruction pair.
choiceNotes: Writing the same value still succeeds.
Correct. It checks whether a write occurred, not the value.
A short sequence of instructions may come in between.

question: Which describes the ABA problem that affects lock-free data structures built with CAS?
choices: Two threads A and B can only run alternately
When a value changes from A to B and back to A, CAS fails to notice the change and succeeds
Two locks A and B are taken in opposite orders
explanation: Suppose a linked list's head pointer is A. While one thread reads A and prepares a CAS, other threads remove A, do work involving B, and reinsert a node at the same address A. The CAS succeeds because the value is still A, but the list has already changed and its structure is corrupted. It is prevented by pairing the pointer with a modification counter compared together, or by using LR/SC.
choiceNotes: It is not about execution order.
Correct. It is a weakness of CAS comparing values only.
That causes deadlock.

question: What does a fetch-and-add instruction, such as RISC-V amoadd.w or x86 lock xadd, do?
choices: It only reads memory and does the addition in a register
It adds the values at two memory addresses and writes the sum to a third
It atomically adds a given number to a memory value and returns the value before the addition
explanation: Fetch-and-add performs the read, add and write as one atomic operation, so a single instruction fixes the counter++ data race. Because it returns the value before the addition, it can also hand out tickets in order, such as assigning each thread a unique number. With no failure and retry, unlike a CAS loop, it performs better when many threads update at once.
choiceNotes: The add and the memory write are both done atomically.
It is not a memory-to-memory operation.
Correct. It suits shared counters.

question: Which describes a spinlock?
choices: A lock that puts the thread to sleep until the OS wakes it when the lock is free
A lock that waits by repeatedly checking the lock variable in a loop until it is free
A mechanism that protects data by spinning a disk
explanation: A spinlock tries to acquire the lock with an atomic instruction and, if that fails, immediately tries again, over and over. There is no cost of calling the OS to sleep and wake, so it is fast when the lock is held only very briefly. It is common inside OS kernels and for mutual exclusion with interrupt handlers. Its drawback is that it keeps using the CPU while waiting.
choiceNotes: Sleeping while waiting is what a mutex typically does.
Correct. It spins while waiting.
It has nothing to do with disks.

question: In which situation is a spinlock least suitable?
choices: When the lock is held for a long time, so waiting threads waste CPU time spinning
When the lock is held only for tens of nanoseconds
Inside an OS kernel, in code that is not allowed to sleep
explanation: A thread waiting on a spinlock keeps using the CPU until the lock is free. If the lock is held for long, all that CPU time is wasted and other threads are held back. On a single core it is worse: the lock cannot be released unless the holder runs, so the waiter spins until its time slice ends. Long waits call for a mutex that sleeps, and some locks spin briefly before sleeping.
choiceNotes: Correct. A lock that sleeps is more efficient then.
Short holds are exactly where spinlocks shine.
Spinlocks are used where sleeping is not allowed.

question: Why does a spinlock usually wait with ordinary reads and use an atomic instruction only when the lock looks free (test-and-test-and-set), instead of retrying the atomic write directly?
choices: Because ordinary reads are more accurate than atomic instructions
Because an atomic instruction may be used only once per program
Reads can wait inside the core's own cache, greatly reducing coherence traffic as the line bounces between cores
explanation: An atomic instruction involves a write, so waiting threads that keep executing it fight to own the line in the M state and keep invalidating others' copies. With ordinary reads, each core just keeps reading its Shared copy in its own cache, generating no traffic. Only when the lock is released and the value changes does a thread try to grab it with an atomic instruction.
choiceNotes: It is not about accuracy.
There is no such limit.
Correct. Waiters stop fighting over the line on every attempt.

question: Which correctly compares a mutex (a lock that sleeps while waiting) with a spinlock?
choices: A mutex gives up the CPU while waiting, which suits long waits, but sleeping and waking cost OS work
A mutex keeps using the CPU while waiting, so it suits only short waits
They are the same thing under different names
explanation: When a mutex cannot be acquired, the thread is put into a waiting state and the CPU goes to other threads; the OS wakes it when the lock is released. It wastes no CPU while waiting, so it suits long waits, but sleeping, waking and the context switch cost several microseconds. Real library mutexes combine both strengths, for example by spinning briefly before sleeping.
choiceNotes: Correct. The choice depends on how long the wait is.
That describes a spinlock.
They differ in how they wait.

question: Which is an example of deadlock?
choices: Thread 1 holds lock A and waits for lock B, while thread 2 holds lock B and waits for lock A
Two threads update the same variable without synchronization and corrupt it
One thread acquires a lock and releases it immediately
explanation: Deadlock is a state in which threads each hold a resource while waiting for one held by another, so none can proceed. In the example, thread 1 waits for B to be released and thread 2 waits for A, but neither gives up its own lock, so both stop forever. Because they stop without using the CPU, the program simply appears frozen.
choiceNotes: Correct. Each waits on the other forever.
That is a data race.
That is normal, harmless use.

question: In a program using several locks, what is the most common way to prevent deadlock?
choices: Fix a single global order in which every thread acquires locks
Never release a lock once acquired
Limit the program to two threads or fewer
explanation: Deadlock arises when threads form a cycle, each waiting for a lock held by another. If everyone follows "always take A before B", no thread can hold B while waiting for A, so no cycle forms. Other methods include acquiring all needed locks at once, or releasing held locks and retrying when a lock cannot be obtained.
choiceNotes: Correct. No cycle of waiting can form.
Without release, other threads wait forever.
Deadlock can happen with just two threads.

question: What does a memory consistency model define?
choices: The cache line size and the number of sets
The kind of transistors used in main-memory DRAM
In what order a core's reads and writes to multiple addresses may be observed by other cores
explanation: For performance, CPUs may reorder memory operations, for example by holding writes in a store buffer or performing reads early. They are designed so that results within one core are unchanged, but other cores may observe the operations in a different order. A memory consistency model defines which reorderings can occur and is the contract that lets programmers write correct synchronization.
choiceNotes: That is cache organization.
It has nothing to do with circuit technology.
Correct. It is a contract between hardware and programmers.

question: Which describes sequential consistency?
choices: Each core's operations run in a random order every time
All cores' operations appear in some single order in which each core's operations occur in program order
All operations run on a single core only
explanation: Under sequential consistency, the operations of all cores appear interleaved into one sequence, like shuffling cards, with each core's operations keeping their program order within it. It is the easiest model for programmers, but it severely limits hardware optimizations such as reordering through store buffers, so most real CPUs adopt looser models.
choiceNotes: Program order is preserved, not randomized.
Correct. It is the most intuitive model.
It assumes multiple cores.

question: The two threads above run simultaneously on different cores (assume no compiler reordering). Which outcome cannot occur under sequential consistency but can occur on real CPUs such as x86?
choices: r1 = 1 and r2 = 1
r1 = 0 and r2 = 1
r1 = 0 and r2 = 0
explanation: Under sequential consistency one of the writes happens first, so at least one read must see 1. On real CPUs, however, x = 1 first enters the core's store buffer, and before it becomes visible to other cores the later read r1 = y can fetch its value from cache or memory. If both cores do this, both read 0. A memory barrier between the write and the read prevents it.
choiceNotes: This occurs under sequential consistency if both writes finish first.
This occurs under sequential consistency if thread 1 finishes first.
Correct. Reads proceed while the writes sit in store buffers.

question: What is a characteristic of the x86 memory consistency model (TSO, total store order)?
choices: It is the weakest model, allowing every combination of reordering
It is exactly sequential consistency, allowing no reordering at all
It is a relatively strong model that allows only a later read of a different address to appear before an earlier write
explanation: Under TSO, writes stay ordered with writes, reads with reads, and a write after a read stays ordered; only a read of a different address may overtake an earlier write. This model directly reflects the presence of a store buffer. Many programs behave intuitively within these limits, so barriers are needed relatively rarely on x86.
choiceNotes: That is closer to weak models such as Arm or RISC-V.
Write-then-read reordering does occur.
Correct. Only the reordering caused by the store buffer is visible.

question: Which statement is correct about weak memory consistency models such as those of Arm and RISC-V (RVWMO)?
choices: They allow many reorderings of accesses to different addresses, and programs insert barriers where order is needed
They allow no reordering, so barrier instructions do not exist
They do not even guarantee ordering of accesses to the same address
explanation: Weak models let hardware reorder fairly freely reads and writes to different addresses that have no dependence. This simplifies circuits and helps performance and power efficiency, but when passing data to other cores, order must be stated explicitly with fence instructions or with loads and stores carrying acquire or release semantics. In high-level languages, using atomic variables makes the compiler emit the right instructions.
choiceNotes: Correct. Hardware gains freedom, and ordering is requested explicitly.
RISC-V has the fence instruction.
Ordering to the same address is maintained by coherence.

question: What is the role of a memory barrier (fence) instruction?
choices: It guarantees that memory operations before the barrier become visible to other cores before those after it
It physically partitions memory and forbids access
It stops the program until every thread arrives
explanation: CPUs can reorder memory operations, so passing data to other cores in a fixed order requires an instruction that prevents it. A memory barrier makes all earlier reads and writes complete (become visible to other cores) before later ones are performed. Lock acquisition and release include this barrier effect, which is why variables protected by a lock are passed correctly.
choiceNotes: Correct. It stops memory operations from being reordered across it.
Forbidding access is done by page protection and similar.
That is barrier synchronization among threads.

question: In the code above, thread 1 prepares data and then signals with flag, and thread 2 waits for flag and then reads data. On a CPU with a weak memory model, what is needed for thread 2 to reliably read 42?
choices: Change the type of data from int to long
Make the write to flag a release and the read of flag an acquire to guarantee the order
Make sure thread 2's loop body is empty
explanation: Under a weak model, thread 1's two writes may appear reordered, or thread 2's read of data may happen before its read of flag, so data might still be stale even though flag is 1. Making the write to flag a release guarantees that earlier writes become visible first, and making the read of flag an acquire keeps later reads from running ahead of it.
choiceNotes: Changing the type does not guarantee order.
Correct. data's write is guaranteed to be visible before flag's.
The loop body has nothing to do with ordering.

question: Which statement is correct about memory operations with acquire and release semantics?
choices: Both acquire and release are the heaviest barriers, completely stopping all reads and writes
Acquire allocates memory and release frees it
Reads and writes after an acquire cannot move before it, and reads and writes before a release cannot move after it
explanation: Taking a lock has acquire semantics and releasing it has release semantics. Operations after the acquire do not leak to before the lock is taken, and operations before the release do not leak to after it is released, so accesses in the protected region stay inside it. With fewer restrictions than a full barrier, which blocks both directions, hardware can keep the remaining reorderings for performance.
choiceNotes: They restrict only one direction, so they are lighter than a full barrier.
This is unrelated to memory allocation.
Correct. It is a lighter, one-directional ordering guarantee.

question: In C, why is marking a flag variable shared between threads volatile not sufficient for synchronization?
choices: A volatile variable can no longer be read by other threads
volatile only restrains compiler optimizations and guarantees neither atomicity nor the order in which other cores see operations
A volatile variable is stored on disk and becomes slow
explanation: volatile tells the compiler not to omit or merge reads and writes of a variable; it was designed for accessing hardware registers. It does not stop the CPU from reordering memory operations, and it does not make operations such as counter++ atomic. Since C11 and C++11, _Atomic and std::atomic guarantee both atomicity and memory ordering.
choiceNotes: Other threads can still read it.
Correct. Use atomic variables for inter-thread synchronization.
It is never stored on disk.

question: Why do C11 _Atomic and C++11 std::atomic let programmers specify a memory order?
choices: To specify where in memory the atomic variable is placed
Choosing only the ordering guarantee needed avoids unnecessary barriers and preserves performance
To fix the order in which threads run in advance
explanation: Atomic operations default to sequential consistency (memory_order_seq_cst), which is easiest to reason about but costs the most in barriers. A simple counter only needs atomicity, so relaxed suffices; a flag that hands off data needs only acquire and release. The compiler emits the minimum instructions the CPU's memory model requires for the chosen order.
choiceNotes: It does not specify placement.
Correct. The default is the strongest, sequential consistency.
It does not decide thread execution order.

question: Which correctly compares coarse-grained locking (one lock for a whole large data structure) with fine-grained locking (separate locks for each part)?
choices: Coarse-grained locking always gives more parallelism
Fine-grained locking reduces the number of locks
Fine-grained locking lets threads use different parts concurrently for more parallelism, but design is harder and deadlock risk grows
explanation: A coarse lock is simple and hard to get wrong, but threads using unrelated parts still wait for each other, so adding cores helps little. Finer granularity, such as one lock per hash-table bucket, lets different parts be operated on simultaneously. But situations requiring several locks increase, and managing acquisition order and the overhead of the locks themselves become issues.
choiceNotes: With a coarse lock, only one thread can enter at a time.
The number of locks increases.
Correct. The choice balances simplicity against parallelism.

question: What property does a lock-free algorithm have?
choices: Even if some thread stops partway, at least one of the other threads can still make progress
Every thread always finishes in a fixed number of steps
Shared data is updated without any atomic instructions
explanation: With locks, if the holder is stalled by an interrupt or low priority, everyone else waits. A lock-free algorithm updates shared data directly with CAS or similar, arranged so that a thread fails and retries only when some other thread has succeeded. As a whole, some thread always makes progress. Building one correctly is hard, though, and pitfalls such as the ABA problem must be handled.
choiceNotes: Correct. There is no thread that can stall everyone while holding a lock.
That is the stronger wait-free property.
It is built with atomic instructions such as CAS.

question: Which describes a critical section?
choices: A part of a program that operates on shared data and must be executed by only one thread at a time
The part of a program that takes the longest time to run
A part that runs only when an error occurs
explanation: If several threads simultaneously execute code that reads and updates a shared variable, a data race occurs. Such a part, which only one thread should run at a time, is called a critical section and is protected by taking a lock before entering and releasing it on exit. The longer the critical section, the longer other threads wait, so it should be kept as short as possible.
choiceNotes: Correct. It is protected with a lock or similar.
It is not defined by how long it takes.
It is not error handling.

question: Which describes barrier synchronization in parallel programs?
choices: It creates a region that only one thread can enter at a time
Threads that arrive first wait at that point until all threads have arrived
An instruction that stops memory operations from being reordered
explanation: In simulations and similar work, all threads must finish one step's computation before moving to the next. With barrier synchronization, each thread stops at the barrier, and when the last thread arrives they all proceed. If the workload is uneven, fast threads spend more time waiting for slow ones, so dividing work evenly matters for performance.
choiceNotes: That is mutual exclusion with a lock.
Correct. It keeps everyone in step phase by phase.
That is a memory barrier, a different thing with a similar name.

question: When 64 cores continuously update one shared counter with atomic instructions, adding cores does not speed things up. What is the main reason?
choices: Atomic instructions can execute on only one core
With many cores the counter value automatically gets smaller
The counter's cache line moves from core to core, so updates proceed only one at a time
explanation: An atomic update requires the core to own the line in the M state, so the line migrates to another core on every update. Each migration costs inter-core communication time, and only one core can update at a time, so adding cores just lengthens the wait. The fix is to reduce shared writes, for example by having each core count locally and summing at the end.
choiceNotes: Any core can execute them.
The value does not change by itself.
Correct. Contention for the line determines performance.

question: Which describes a NUMA (non-uniform memory access) system?
choices: Every core reaches all memory in the same time
Each core has near and far memory, and accessing far memory takes longer
Each core can read only its own memory and cannot use other cores' memory
explanation: In servers with multiple CPU sockets, for example, each socket has memory attached directly, and other sockets' memory is reached over inter-socket links. Far memory is therefore slower and has less bandwidth than near memory. All memory appears in one address space, so programs run unchanged, but placing data and threads on the same side improves performance.
choiceNotes: That is uniform memory access (UMA).
Correct. Placing data in near memory matters.
Far memory is accessible, just slower.

question: Under the first-touch policy common on Linux NUMA systems (a page is placed in the memory of the node where the thread first writing it runs), what should programmers watch out for?
choices: Under first touch pages are placed on random nodes
All page placements are fixed when malloc is called
If one thread zero-initializes a large array, all of it lands on one node, and threads on other nodes end up using far memory
explanation: malloc alone assigns no physical pages; the page fault on first write places each page in the memory of the node where the writing thread runs. So if one thread does the initialization, the whole array gathers on that node, and in the parallel computation much of each thread's portion is in far memory. Initializing in parallel with the same division of work as the computation puts each portion near its thread.
choiceNotes: It is not random; the first thread to touch decides.
Placement happens at first write, not at malloc.
Correct. Initialization should be split among the threads that later use the data.

question: Which is NOT a reason a parallel program fails to scale as cores are added?
choices: Frequent synchronization between threads, such as lock waits
Large imbalance in the amount of work per thread
Each thread reads and writes only its own private data
explanation: The main obstacles to parallel speedup include parts that cannot be parallelized (Amdahl's law), waits on locks and barriers, cache lines bouncing due to shared data or false sharing, load imbalance and insufficient memory bandwidth. If each thread works only on its own private data, there is no communication or waiting with other threads, which approaches ideal parallel scaling.
choiceNotes: Synchronization waits are a classic scaling limit.
Imbalance creates time spent waiting for slow threads.
Correct. Private data alone does not hinder scaling.

question: When splitting loop iterations among threads, which division suits iterations whose costs vary widely?
choices: Static assignment, dividing iterations evenly by count at the start and never adjusting
Giving every iteration to a single thread
Dynamic assignment, where work is split into small chunks and idle threads grab the next chunk
explanation: Static assignment has little overhead, but if iterations differ in cost, the threads that drew heavy parts lag while the rest wait. With dynamic assignment, threads take the next piece of work from a shared counter or similar, so faster threads take on more and the load evens out. Chunks that are too small increase the overhead of fetching work, so their size must be tuned.
choiceNotes: Equal counts with unequal costs leave imbalance.
That is not parallelization at all.
Correct. It evens out imbalance automatically.

question: When several threads sum all elements of an array, which approach performs well?
choices: Every thread adds each element to one shared variable, taking a lock each time
Every thread adds each element to one shared variable without synchronization
Each thread sums its share in a local variable, and the partial sums are added once each at the end
explanation: Updating a shared variable per element is very slow because of lock or atomic waits and cache lines bouncing between cores. If each thread computes a partial sum in a register or local variable and the total is formed with just one addition per thread at the end, shared writes become negligible. This approach is called a reduction and is built into parallel frameworks such as OpenMP.
choiceNotes: Lock waits and communication nearly eliminate the benefit.
A data race makes the total wrong.
Correct. This is called a reduction.

question: What is a characteristic of a reader-writer lock?
choices: Any number of writers may enter together, but only one reader
Any number of readers may enter together, but a writer enters alone, excluding everyone else
Only one thread may enter, whether reading or writing
explanation: Concurrent reads cannot corrupt data, so a reader-writer lock lets readers run together and makes only writers exclusive. It raises parallelism for data that is read often and changed rarely, such as a configuration table. If readers keep arriving, though, a writer may never get in, so some implementations give writers priority.
choiceNotes: It is the other way around.
Correct. It suits data that is mostly read.
That is an ordinary lock (mutex).

question: What is the most suitable use of a counting semaphore?
choices: Always doubling the value of a variable
Merging all program execution into a single thread
Letting up to four threads at a time use a resource with a fixed number of units, such as four connections
explanation: A semaphore holds a counter of remaining units: a thread decrements it before use (waiting if it is 0) and increments it when done. With an initial value of 4, up to four threads can use the resource at once. With 1, it works like a lock for mutual exclusion. Waiting threads are usually put to sleep and woken by the OS.
choiceNotes: It does not compute values.
It limits parallelism but does not merge everything into one thread.
Correct. The counter tracks how many units remain.

question: What is the difference between cache coherence and a memory consistency model?
choices: They mean the same thing under different names
Coherence keeps values at the same address consistent; a consistency model governs the order in which operations on different addresses appear
Coherence is purely software, and consistency purely hardware
explanation: Coherence guarantees, for any single address, that all cores see its writes in the same order and eventually read the latest value. A consistency model specifies, when core 0 writes x and then y, in what orders other cores may observe those writes. Even with coherence, writes to different addresses can appear reordered, which is where barriers are needed.
choiceNotes: They address different problems.
Correct. Both are needed to write correct parallel programs.
Both involve hardware and software.

question: Which describes the idea of hardware transactional memory?
choices: Critical sections run speculatively; with no conflict with other threads they commit as a whole, and on conflict they abort and retry
All memory reads and writes are logged to disk like bank transactions
Memory writes are forbidden and only reads are allowed
explanation: In transactional memory, a critical section runs as a transaction whose writes stay tentative and invisible to others. If no other thread touched the same data, all writes commit at once at the end; on conflict, everything is rolled back and retried or the code falls back to an ordinary lock. When conflicts are rare, even coarse locks can achieve parallelism close to fine-grained locking.
choiceNotes: Correct. It can sometimes run in parallel without taking the lock.
It has nothing to do with logging to disk.
Writes are performed too.

question: When waiting on a condition variable until a queue becomes non-empty, why is the condition rechecked in a while loop rather than an if after waking?
choices: A while loop runs faster than an if statement
Condition variables cannot be used with if statements
Even after waking, another thread may have taken the item first or the wake-up may be spurious, so the condition may not hold
explanation: Waiting on a condition variable releases the lock and sleeps; when signaled, the thread reacquires the lock and returns. But before it does, another thread may grab the lock and take the queue element. Implementations are also allowed to wake a thread with no signal at all (a spurious wake-up). So the code checks the condition after waking and waits again if it does not hold, using a while loop.
choiceNotes: It is not about speed.
There is no such rule.
Correct. The condition must be rechecked after waking.
